summary:
Horus NASA Timeline is a bilingual (EN / PT-BR) interactive web platform that transforms the history of spacecraft hardware left behind by NASA since the 1960s into an engaging visual and audio experience for school-age students.
To connect this engineering hardware with the science it enabled, we built a navigable 3D Solar System observatory featuring planetary surface maps and markers anchored to official landing and trajectory coordinates across the Moon, Mars, Asteroids 433 Eros and 4 Vesta, Dwarf Planet 1 Ceres, heliocentric orbit, and interstellar space, alongside Earth's permanent NSSDCA archive. The platform combines a chronological timeline of 64 milestones (1966–2026) — tracking each mission from launch to its current operational or dormant state — with an auto-advancing Guided Tour synchronized to spatial soundscapes and authentic NASA recordings, official NASA/USGS 3D spacecraft models, 2.5D archival photo galleries, and an interactive 72-flight telemetry explorer for the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter.
By replacing static lists of facts with a browser-based interactive exploration, the project helps spark scientific curiosity in young learners and brings students closer to aerospace engineering and planetary science. 
Built strictly from verified NASA and NSSDCA datasets and media — with zero fabricated 3D meshes or data — it ensures scientific integrity while remaining freely accessible worldwide in English and Portuguese.
details:
• What the project does and how it works: The Horus NASA Timeline is an interactive web platform that explores the history of NASA missions to the Moon, Mars, asteroids, Ceres, and deep space, spanning the period from 1966 to 2026. The platform combines a 3D Solar System Observatory with a timeline of 64 historical milestones. Users can explore different destinations, locate probes and instruments on the surfaces of celestial bodies, or follow a guided tour through the major events of space exploration. The project brings together 13 missions, in addition to providing access to the NSSDCA archive. Each mission has its own dedicated section featuring interactive 3D models or 2.5D scenes built from real NASA imagery, historical audio recordings, and photo galleries. We also included an interactive visualization of the 72 flights completed by the Ingenuity helicopter on Mars. The platform is initially available in English, with the option to switch the language to Brazilian Portuguese.
  • Benefits and expected impact: Our main goal was to make NASA’s scientific and historical archives more accessible and engaging, especially for students and anyone curious about space exploration. Much of this information is scattered across technical documents, databases, and different mission webpages. Therefore, we sought to gather it all in a single environment, providing a more visual and interactive experience. We wanted to make it easier to understand not only the destinations of these missions, but also their achievements and the ongoing importance they hold for science. By connecting engineering, history, and scientific discoveries, we hope to spark curiosity about space and encourage greater interest among young people in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fields. Furthermore, the entire experience runs directly in the browser, with no installation or account creation required.
  • Tools, programming languages, and software used: We developed the platform using TypeScript (ES2022), HTML5, CSS3, JSON, and Markdown, along with Python 3 scripts for data validation. To build the three-dimensional environments, we used Three.js and WebGL 2.0, which enable the visualization and interaction with spacecraft models, camera movement, and exploration of celestial bodies. We also used the Web Audio API for sound features, SVG for interactive visualizations, and WebAssembly-based Draco technology to load compressed 3D models. During development, we worked with Node.js and npm, FFmpeg for audio processing, and Pillow for image optimization. The platform was deployed using Firebase Hosting, with security measures such as a strict Content Security Policy. We also used Gemini as a supporting tool to organize and structure the mission data.
  • Creativity: One of our main decisions during development was to create an experience that resembled a space observatory rather than a traditional website. We chose a dark visual identity inspired by spacecraft interfaces and mission control centers, combining interactive three-dimensional environments with 2.5D scenes built from historical NASA photographs. When official 3D models were not available, we chose to use real mission images instead of creating representations that might not match the original characteristics of the spacecraft. This allowed us to preserve the visual experience without compromising fidelity to scientific information. Sound was also an important part of the project. We integrated real recordings made available by NASA, ambient sounds, and subtle interface effects to make the exploration more immersive. The audio system automatically adjusts the volume of background sounds whenever a historical recording is played.
  • Factors considered during development: Scientific accuracy was one of our top priorities. We worked with official NASA sources, avoided including unverified information, and added disclaimers whenever object distances or dimensions were not represented to true scale. We also included source credits and licensing information for the materials used. Performance was another key factor. Since the platform brings together 3D models, images, and audio files, we took care to optimize these assets and implement on-demand loading, avoiding unnecessary downloads. Through this process, we reduced the file size from approximately 207 MB to 42.33 MB in the project's public folder. We also considered accessibility through bilingual navigation, compatibility with modern browsers, and application security, including content restrictions and validation of URLs used in Markdown files. Throughout development, we sought to strike a balance between visual quality, technical performance, and scientific reliability without making the platform complicated to use.
